title: Request-Path Compensation Cascades Across Fallible Operations
pattern: A primary operation performs fallible synchronous compensation to undo earlier database or remote work, or an upstream service explicitly chains downstream undo calls as part of request-path recovery.
why_bad: A failing compensation can leave partial effects and obscure the original failure. Long recovery chains tie up request lifetimes and couple upstream orchestration to downstream lifecycle and rollback details, so a change in a downstream interface or transactional model breaks the whole upstream chain and prevents independent evolution.
detection: Inspect error paths after multi-step effects for inline database mutations or remote undo calls. Distinguish two subcases: (1) the general compensation cascade, where an inline error-recovery block performs synchronous database or remote mutations to undo previous steps; (2) the cross-service case, where an orchestration function performing multiple sequential remote calls has error blocks that explicitly trigger compensating undo operations on previously invoked systems, so orchestration depends on downstream rollback states. An awaited async call still belongs to a synchronously dependent request workflow when its completion blocks the next recovery step.
counterexample: A genuine database transaction that atomically rolls back the participating changes without manual compensation code. A deliberately chosen low-scale design using database-level distributed transactions (2PC) may be acceptable, though it limits overall scalability. Simple local cleanup is not automatically a distributed compensation cascade.
fix: Use one real transaction where the effects fit its atomic boundary. Otherwise coordinate through a durable workflow/saga, transactional outbox, event-driven orchestration, centralized workflow manager, or background job queue that records required compensation and its outcome independently of the request. Define explicit service-level compensation contracts and handle failed compensation without losing the initiating failure; merely moving calls to an untracked task is not a correctness repair.
source: Juval Löwy, *Righting Software*, Chapter 2.; Righting Software, Chapter 2, "Decomposition - Services Bloating and Coupling" [59, 60]
